newsitem.title: UK: IRA keeps N.Ireland waiting for truce decision.
newsitem.headline: IRA keeps N.Ireland waiting for truce decision.

text.p: The IRA kept Northern Ireland guessing on Saturday about when it might call a new ceasefire to earn its Sinn Fein political wing a seat at floundering peace talks.

Sinn Fein president Gerry Adams raised the province's hopes on Friday when he said he had urged his Irish Republican Army allies to call a halt to their war against British rule to allow him to take part in negotiations on a political settlement.
"The IRA leadership assured us that they would respond without delay to our request," he said in a statement.
Political opponents of the guerrillas said they expected the IRA would accede to Adams's demand. Rank and file republicans said they expected an IRA annoucement sometime this weekend.
Media reports across the divided island were optimistic. Some said the ceasefire announcement would be on Saturday.

There was no word from Sin Fein or the guerrillas themselves. Sinn Fein vice-president Pat Doherty made clear that Britain had allayed the party's concerns about terms for its entry to all-party talks, including a guarantee that demands for an IRA arms surrender would not be allowed to block talks progress.

"We feel that to some extent they have been resolved, in terms of (our) entry, in terms of the time-scale for the talks, the fact that (arms) decommissioning as as barrier to entry has been removed, and that there is some belief that confidence-building measures (by Britain) would flow from this process," he told BBC radio.
Doherty's comments echoed remarks by Adams that signalled his belief that Britain and Ireland, co-sponsors of the talks, were committed to "inclusive and meaningful negotiations".
Sceptical Protestant politicians, who represent Northern Ireland's 60 per cent majority and want continued British rule, accused London of pandering to republican pressure.
David Trimble, leader of the main Ulster Unionist Party (UUP), will meet British Prime Minister Tony Blair in London on Monday to find out what concessions have been made to Sinn Fein.
The UUPs's Jeffrey Donaldson told Reuters: "We are deeply concerned that the government has done a secret deal with the IRA to secure another ceasefire."

For the past two years the IRA has baulked at any demand that it hand over the Semtex plastic explosive and arsenal of automatic weapons it has used to attack what it sees as Britain's occupation of a part of Ireland.
Political sources said that Blair would try allay Trimble's worries that British and Irish plans to achieve guerrilla disarament in a gradual process alongside talks are too vague.

Unionists are threatening to oppose Anglo-Irish "decommissioning" proposals in a vote at multi-party talks peace talks on Wednesday, which would be a severe setback for hopes of early political progress.

Sinn Fein is currently barred from the negotiations because of the IRA's continued war against Britain. The IRA shot and wounded five members of a joint army and police patrol this month and murdered two policeman in Lurgan in June.
Irish Prime Minister Bertie Ahern said he welcomed Adams' decision to go to the IRA to seek a fresh cessation of violence.
"I trust and hope that their response will be positive as this would be very good news for all the people of Ireland....
"We must all unite to consolidate peace and to ensure that the gun in Irish politics is silenced for the last time."

But Unionist politicians said they suspected any ceasefire would be a rerun of a a 17-month truce which the IRA ended in Fenbruary last year when it bombed targets in London and Machester after failing to win Sinn Fein a seat at the talks.
